# Visayhajātaka (Ja 340)

**ID:** Ja 340
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Visayhajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Merchant Visayha
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja340
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Visayhajātaka* (Ja 340) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection recounting the Bodhisatta's perfection of generosity (*dānapāramī*) [Warren 1896; SuttaCentral]. According to the frame story, the Buddha related this past birth while dwelling at Jetavana to comfort the wealthy householder Anāthapiṇḍika, referring back to the events of the *Khadiraṅgāra-jātaka* to illustrate how the wise of old maintained their charitable vows despite supernatural opposition [SuttaCentral; Cowell 1897; Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was born in Benares as the great guildmaster Visayha, possessing eighty crores of wealth and observing the five moral precepts [Cowell 1897; Amore & Shinn 1981]. He established six distribution halls—at the four city gates, in the city center, and at the doorway of his own estate—where hundreds of thousands of supplicants were fed daily [Law 1926; Cowell 1897].

Visayha's boundless charity disturbed Sakka, king of heaven, whose throne grew hot from the power of the Bodhisatta's merit [Cowell 1897; Amore & Shinn 1981]. Fearing displacement from his heavenly office, Sakka caused all of Visayha's stored provisions, treasures, and retinue to vanish [Cowell 1897; Clark 1994]. Reduced to extreme poverty, Visayha gathered and sold grass to feed his wife and give alms, eventually giving away his final meager coins and collapsing from hunger [Amore & Shinn 1981]. Sakka appeared in mid-air to counsel the merchant to preserve his remaining goods and abandon his gifts, but Visayha rejected the god's advice, explaining that his boundless charity was undertaken not for celestial sovereignty or worldly power, but solely for the realization of supreme Buddhahood [Fausböll 1883; Narada 2008; War Yar Mein Da 2015].

DharmaNexus identifies extensive internal reuse between the canonical text and the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (matching four passages across 592 characters, particularly §2.1–4.4) [DharmaNexus]. Beyond Pali literature, the narrative directly corresponds to the story of Avisahya, the fifth tale in Āryaśūra's Sanskrit *Jātakamālā*, whose Tibetan translation (Degé D4150) is aligned by DharmaNexus with seven matching passages [Speyer 1895; Clark 1994; DharmaNexus].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Tatiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a3) (§2.1–4.4 ↔ §1033_3–1042)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): སྐྱེས་པའི་རབས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུད། (jātakamāla) (D4150) [bo]

- [Cowell 1897] E. B. Cowell, The Jātaka, or Stories of the Buddha's Former Births, Vol. III (1897) — Summary of the frame story, Visayha's almsgiving halls, Sakka's anxiety, and the disappearance of wealth.

- [Amore & Shinn 1981] Roy C. Amore & Larry D. Shinn, Lustful Maidens and Ascetic Kings (1981) — Retelling of Visayha's destitution, cutting hay, giving away his earnings, and Sakka's temptation.
- [Clark 1994] Robert Warren Clark, Māra: Psychopathology and Evil in the Buddhism of India and Tibet (1994) — Concordance of Ja 340 with Jātakamālā tale no. 5 and Sakka's testing role.
- [Speyer 1895] J. S. Speyer (tr.), The Jātakamālā or Garland of Birth-Stories by Āryaśūra (1895) — Etymology and Sanskrit parallel of Visayha as Avisahya.
- [Narada 2008] Narada Mahathera, The Buddha and His Teachings (Revised 2008) — Doctrinal context of the Bodhisatta's conscious striving for supreme Buddhahood in Ja 340.
- [War Yar Mein Da 2015] War Yar Mein Da, Pāramīs / Pāramitās in Theravada and Mahayana (2015) — Identification as Visayha Setthi Jātaka illustrating Dānapāramī for Buddhahood.
- [Warren 1896] Henry Clarke Warren, Buddhism in Translations (1896) — Listing of Visayha the treasurer among the fulfillers of the perfection of almsgiving.
